# HTML response built from HTTP request data (Python)

`qualor:python/xss` · Issue · Severity: High · [CWE-79](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/79.html) · OWASP Top 10: [A05:2025 Injection](https://top10.owasp.org/2025/A05_2025-Injection/), [A03:2021 Injection](https://top10.owasp.org/2021/A03_2021-Injection/)

## What it finds

<!-- begin: what-it-finds -->
HTTP request data written into an HTML response without escaping:

- returned as the body of a Flask view, `make_response()` or `Response()`, a Django
  `HttpResponse`, a Starlette or FastAPI `HTMLResponse`, or a FastAPI path operation declared with
  `response_class=HTMLResponse`;
- wrapped in `Markup()`, `mark_safe()` or `SafeString()`, which switch escaping off, or used as the
  format string of `format_html()`.

Autoescaping templates (`render_template()`, Django's `render()`), JSON responses and escaped values
are not reported. Neither is the output of a command that request data chose, nor the content of a
file it named: those are the findings of the command-injection and path-traversal rules. The
output of a fixed program given request data (`echo`) and a page fetched from a URL the request
chooses still count as request data; a page fetched from a fixed origin
(`"https://api.example.com/items/" + item`) does not.
<!-- end: what-it-finds -->

## Why it matters

<!-- begin: why-it-matters -->
Markup in the value becomes part of the page. A value such as `<script>...</script>` runs in the
browser of everyone who opens the link or page: it can read what the user sees, act in their name
and steal data that scripts can reach.
<!-- end: why-it-matters -->

## Example

<!-- begin: example -->
**Noncompliant:** a Django view pastes the name into HTML.

```python
from django.http import HttpResponse


def hello(request):
    name = request.GET.get("name", "")
    return HttpResponse("<p>Hello, " + name + "</p>")
```

**Compliant:** `format_html()` escapes the value before inserting it.

```python
from django.http import HttpResponse
from django.utils.html import format_html


def hello(request):
    name = request.GET.get("name", "")
    return HttpResponse(format_html("<p>Hello, {}</p>", name))
```
<!-- end: example -->

## How to fix

<!-- begin: how-to-fix -->
- Render HTML through an autoescaping template: Flask's `render_template()`, Django's `render()`.
- Or escape the value: `markupsafe.escape()`, `html.escape()`, Django's `escape()` or
  `format_html("...{}...", value)`. For HTML that users may write, sanitise it with `nh3` or
  `bleach`.
- Where no HTML is meant, send JSON (`jsonify()`, `JsonResponse`) or `text/plain`.
- Never wrap request data in `Markup()`, `mark_safe()` or `SafeString()`.
<!-- end: how-to-fix -->

## Frameworks and APIs covered

- Flask
- Django
- FastAPI
- Starlette
- MarkupSafe
- bleach
- nh3

## Known limits

<!-- begin: known-limits -->
- A Flask view is recognised by its `route()`/`get()`/`post()` decorator in a module that imports
  Flask; class-based Flask views (`MethodView`) are not followed.
- A response body must be visibly text (a name, `+`, `%`, an f-string, `str()` or a string
  method). A helper that builds HTML from request data and returns it is not followed, while the
  result of a function of another module that is given request data, kept in a variable and
  returned, is still taken for text.
- Values read from an object a call returned (a database row looked up by a request id) are taken
  for stored data, unless the call receives request data whole; a request value reaching such a
  call through a variable is missed.
- A Flask view returning the request's JSON whole is taken for JSON, also with a `{}` or `[]`
  default (`request.get_json() or {}`, `data = data or {}`, `if data is None: data = {}`); a
  default that is request text, or any other value assigned to the variable, is still reported.
  A request whose JSON body is a bare string is not followed. A response whose content type is
  changed after it is made (`resp.mimetype = "text/plain"`) is still taken for HTML.
- A slice is followed when it slices request data in place (`request.args["q"][:50]`),
  a variable assigned request data, or a view parameter; a slice of a value built from request
  data (`(request.args["q"] + "x")[:50]`), or of a variable assigned again after the request value
  (`q = q.strip()`, also `q = q + request.args["b"]` or a fallback `q = request.form["q"]`), is
  missed. In Starlette and FastAPI middleware only a slice of the request's path written in
  place is followed.
- Request sources are recognised by their shape: a Flask `<int:n>` route parameter and a numeric
  Django URL argument still count as request data, and a function whose first parameter is named
  `request` in a Django module is taken for a view.
- A function named like a class-based view's handler (`get`, `post`, ..., `dispatch`) that takes
  `(self, request, ...)` in a Django module is taken for one also outside a class: its parameters
  after `request` count as URL arguments.
- After a `get()`, `pop()` or `setdefault()` whose key or default is request data, or after an item
  is set to request data (`d["q"] = request.args["q"]`), the object counts as request data for the
  rest of the function, whatever it is (a dict, `os.environ`, a cache, a client): a later lookup of
  a constant entry in it is reported, as is `os.environ.get("HOME")` after
  `os.environ.get(request.args["k"])`. A `get()` called on a call's result
  (`requests.Session().get(url)`) passes no request data on.
- The command positions that make a command's output not count are those the command-injection
  rule reports. A file read by iterating over it (`for line in f`) or through a helper still
  counts as request data. A page fetched through a requests Session or httpx Client held in a
  variable is taken for stored data when an attribute of the response is used
  (`session.get(url).text`). A fixed origin is recognised only as a literal at the start of the
  URL; one held in a module constant (`API_BASE + "/items/" + item`) is not. A response written
  by a function passed to a fixed-origin fetch (a requests response hook) is not checked.
<!-- end: known-limits -->

## Tests

The test file [`rules/python/xss/xss.py`](../../../rules/python/xss/xss.py) holds every case the rule reports or accepts:
lines marked `ruleid:` must be reported and lines marked `ok:` must not. The known limits are
marked `todoruleid:` (missed) and `todook:` (wrongly reported). `npm test` runs them with OpenGrep,
and checks the example above as well.
